Results: A 26-year-old woman with several autoimmune conditions
was referred because of ﬁlamentary keratitis. Conservative manage-
ment using lubrication, mucolytics, and bandage contact lenses
failed to adequately relieve symptoms. Despite the addition of oral
prednisone, cyclosporine, and azathioprine, the patient ’s condition
persisted with numerous ﬁlaments and severe dry eye. One month
later, the patient had an episode of sudden muscle cramps in her
back, for which she was hospitalized. Investigations revealed
a diagnosis of stiff person syndrome, positive for glutamic acid
decarboxylase autoantibodies. Plasmapheresis and high-dose intra-
venous steroids were provided as initial therapy. On follow-up, her
ﬁlamentary keratitis resolved and at the last visit, her ocular
symptoms had completely resolved.

CASE REPORT
A 26-year-old woman was referred with a diagnosis of
ﬁlamentary keratitis. She had several diagnosed autoimmune
conditions including ulcerative colitis, alopecia totalis, Graves
disease, and minimal change disease. She used no oral medi-
cations. At the initial visit, she was asymptomatic and her
uncorrected visual acuity was 20/20 in both eyes. Her cornea
was clear, and her lacrimal lake appeared suf ﬁcient. Her lashes
were noted to be sparse. She was advised to use preservative-free
t e a r sa sn e e d e d .
Two weeks later, the patient presented with a 5-day history of
painful eyes and foreign-body sensation. Slit-lamp examination
revealed bilateral corneal ﬁlaments. The anterior chamber was deep
and quiet, and her uncorrected visual acuity was 20/25 in both eyes.
She had no ptosis or lagophthalmos, and her blinking was normal.
Initial management included bandage contact lenses, acetylcysteine
drops 4 times daily, cyclosporine 0.05% drops twice daily, and
prophylactic antibiotic drops twice daily.
Four weeks later, her ﬁlaments persisted bilaterally. She had
severe dry eye with the Schirmer test value without anesthesia
measuring 0 mm. On suspicion that her autoimmune conditions were
ﬂaring up, she was administered prednisone 5 mg daily, azathioprine

drops 100 mg daily, and cyclosporine 100 mg twice daily by her
rheumatologist. Her ophthalmic drops were unchanged. New
bandage contact lenses were placed, and she was referred to
rheumatology to rule out Sjogren syndrome; however, antibody
testing was not performed. The patient ’s ﬁlaments resolved at
follow-up 4 weeks later but recurred in just 3 days despite the
modiﬁcation to her systemic medications.
One month later, the patient experienced sudden muscle
weakness and back spasms. She was admitted to the hospital and
was diagnosed with SPS positive for glutamic acid decarboxylase
autoantibodies. She received high-dose intravenous corticosteroids
and underwent 5 rounds of plasmapheresis, with plans to receive
rituximab once insurance coverage was obtained. She remained on
oral prednisone, cyclosporine, and azathioprine, with the addition of
baclofen and diazepam for continued symptomatic relief.
Two months later, the patient reported dramatic improvement
of her ﬁlamentary keratitis. Her uncorrected visual acuity was 20/25
in both eyes. Her brows and eyelashes had regrown. Her cornea was
clear, and her tear lake appeared robust. The patient reported rare use
of lubricant drops. She was advised to complete what remained of
her cyclosporine 0.05% drops and follow-up as needed with her
optometrist. She remained on her systemic medications with
intentions for slow tapering.
